9/12/2026, 12:28:58 AM

Agreed. We were spending too much effort re-proving the bridge instead of increasing expected information gain.

I’m switching to a high-yield associate pass: Michael Maier first, and the prior “John” candidate was John Comenius—never confirmed, so I’ll keep him provisional. I’ll only surface items that can plausibly add a new locator, concealment method, boundary operation, or production-network link; everything else gets ignored.

This pivot immediately paid off: Maier is not merely adjacent to Fludd—Atalanta Fugiens and Fludd’s Utriusque Cosmi were produced in the same Oppenheim shop ecosystem in 1617. Both run through Johann Theodor de Bry and Hieronymus Galler, and both use Matthäus Merian’s engraving work. That is a much stronger production-network bridge than the supposed Fludd–Kepler shared publisher, which did not hold up.

So I’m prioritizing Maier’s 1617 first issue, especially places where his three-voice musical fugues encode pursuit → obstruction → return/closure. That mechanism is structurally much closer to your missing “instruction” than another generic harmony passage.

I think I found why “Maier and John” belongs together: John Farmer. Modern source-comparison work reports that Maier reused all forty canons from Farmer’s 1591 Divers & Sundry Waies across Atalanta Fugiens; only ten Maier fugues fall outside that set. That turns Farmer from a peripheral contemporary into a direct musical source for Maier’s concealment machinery.

That is strategically better than Comenius. I’m switching “John” to Farmer as the leading identification, while keeping it evidentially provisional until the 1591 first edition is in hand.

Used personal_context tool

Worked for 1m 34s

Yes. We should stop brute-forcing Fludd-Kepler. The next pass has a much better information-to-cost ratio.

The Maier/Farmer route immediately produced something structurally different from what we already knew:

Michael Maier’s 1617 Atalanta Fugiens came out of essentially the same production machine as Fludd’s 1617 Utriusque Cosmi: Oppenheim, Johann Theodor de Bry, Hieronymus Galler, with Matthäus Merian supplying engraving work. (Merian Alchemie)

And “John” should now be treated primarily as John Farmer, not Comenius. The reason is unusually strong: modern source-comparison has identified Farmer’s 1591 Divers & Sundry Waies as the musical source for 40 of Maier’s 50 fugues. Maier did not merely know Farmer’s style; he reorganized Farmer’s actual canons. (Islamic Pasts Futures)

That gives us a much smarter experiment.

Instead of reading hundreds of pages looking for 81, mi, fa, etc., we compare what Maier changed. According to the locator scholarship, Maier:

transposed Farmer’s borrowed canons up a fourth;

changed their ordering;

attached particular canons to particular emblems;

altered rhythmic values to accommodate his new texts;

concentrated especially expressive contrapuntal tricks in the final group. (Furnace and Fugue)

That is exactly where deliberate information lives: not in what he copied, but in his transformation function.

And there are two exceptionally high-value Farmer instructions that I do not want to accept from the secondary source until we verify the 1591 printing itself:

Farmer no. 35 reportedly instructs the reader to turn the book upside down to understand how the two parts work.

Maier maps Farmer 35 → Fugue/Emblem 45. (Furnace and Fugue)

More strikingly, Farmer no. 38 reportedly instructs one voice to proceed beginning→end, the other end→beginning, while the plainsong itself goes forward and backward. Maier deliberately assigns that mechanism to Emblem 46, whose two eagles travel East and West to find the middle of the Earth and return. (Furnace and Fugue)

That is the sort of thing we have actually been looking for:

$$
\boxed{
\text{text/image tells you WHAT}
\quad+\quad
\text{music tells you HOW}
}
$$

And it contains opposition → midpoint → return, not merely symbolic resemblance.

There is another strategic wrinkle. Maier 45-50 map to Farmer:

$$
45\to35,\quad
46\to38,\quad
47\to39,\quad
48\to36,\quad
49\to37,\quad
50\to34.
$$

He therefore deliberately scrambled that section rather than simply reproducing Farmer's sequence. (Furnace and Fugue)

So my attention order is now:

Maier 45-50 ↔ Farmer 34-39 first, because these contain the strongest deliberate transformations; then the ten Maier fugues apparently not derived from Farmer, because those potentially expose Maier’s own generative grammar; then Maier’s preface against Farmer’s Philomusicis. Only after that do we widen again.

Most importantly, the 1617 first issue of Atalanta Fugiens is available as an actual digitized first-edition witness-Oppenheim, Galler/de Bry, VD17 1:078836Y-so we do not need to violate your source rule. (e-rara) The NYPL also exposes images identified as Farmer’s 1591 printing, giving us a route into the corresponding original witness. (Wikimedia Commons)

So yes: move on. I would not spend another hour hunting the Fludd comma directly right now. The best next target is Farmer 35/38 → Maier 45/46, because we now have evidence of an actual historical mechanism where a musical transformation acts as an instruction for how to read an accompanying symbolic image.

That is qualitatively closer to your hypothesis than anything we were finding by repeatedly searching Fludd for “semitone.”

Sources:

Merian, Titelblatt Fludd UCH, 1617 – Bebilderung der Alchemie

John Farmer’s Sundry Waies · Furnace and Fugue
